newsitem.title: CROATIA: Albright trip puts spotlight on Croatia refugees.
newsitem.headline: Albright trip puts spotlight on Croatia refugees.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright plunged into the heart of Croatia's refugee problem on Saturday, commiserating with people caught up in ethnic tensions and demanding the Croatian government provide compensation.
Albright made a lightning trip to the Krajina region where Serbs and families of mixed ethnic background have suffered attacks, harassment and house-burnings.
She visited displaced familes, a burned out house and tackled Croatia's Reconstruction Minister Jure Radic face-to-face.
"How can you let this kind of thing happen? These poor people did nothing wrong," she told Radic in the yard of a farmhouse in the village of Donji Kukuruzari.
Albright had just met two families of mixed ethnic background -- one Croat-Moslem, one Serb-Croat -- who returned to Krajina two weeks ago to re-occupy their homes.

She flew to the region in U.S. Blackhawk helicopters after a meeting with Croatian President Franjo Tudjman in Zagreb during which she warned his country would face economic and diplomatic penalties if he failed to aid the return of refugees, cooperate in bringing war criminals to justice and comply with other aspects of the Dayton peace accord.
Tudjman insisted Zagreb supported the right of Serbs to return to their homes.

"For all practical purposes, Croatia is not embarking on any policy of ethnic purity but rather recognises fully all human and ethnic rights of all communities living in this country, including Serbs," he said. The Banadinovic and Icitovic families fled from Krajina in 1991 when Serbs pursuing ethnic purity took over the region.

Albright sat at a table in the modest farmhouse as the families explained how they had obtained official Croatian citizenship documents but then faced a lengthy wait if they wanted to return to the region as part of an organised U.N. programme.
Impatient, they decided to skip the bureaucracy and take a ride back to their home town with a friend from Zagreb.
On the night they returned, a mainly Croat mob ransacked the house of one family, burning their belongings and beating the adults in front of their children.
Radic, clearly uncomfortable as he accompanied Albright on her trip, insisted the attack was not organised and suggested the families provoked the violence.

"You should be ashamed," said Albright. "I'll tell you something, it's worse than that. It is the fact that the government at the top is thinking that these kinds of things are normal. It is not normal."
Later, in front of television cameras, Radic condemned the violence and said Croatia was working on the problem.
He said many Croats had also suffered during the war years and yet many non-Croat properties, including homes and churches, remained intact.
Albright, Czech-born and a World War Two refugee, said non-Croat families who wanted to return should be moved back in large groups so they would be less vulnerable to Croat attacks.
U.S. officials said she was trying to put across as clearly as possible the message that "ethnic cleansing" was immoral.
It was important that war refugees should be allowed to return if there was to be lasting peace, said the officials.
